newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Foreign buy could trigger S.African Sanlam listing.
newsitem.headline: Foreign buy could trigger S.African Sanlam listing.

text.p: South African mutual life insurance giant Sanlam could convert to a listed company to help fund a major foreign acquisition, managing director Desmond Smith said on Tuesday.
While Sanlam had no specific acquisition plans at present, Smith said it was busy restructuring to make it a world-class financial services group.

Sanlam chairman Marinus Daling said last year that the Cape Town-based group might demutualise and seek a stock market listing in three to four years. Smith said the most likely trigger for such a move was a big overseas buy.

"A major drive in internationalisation could precipitate that. If one were to acquire a substantial interest in a life office elsewhere which entailed pumping in a lot of capital, it could mean one would have to look for a listing in the process.
"At the moment it is not on our agenda to internationalise our insurance business but we have an open mind," Smith told reporters at a results presentation.

Sanlam would need a compelling reason to demutualise and would also need to make an attractive offer to policyholders, Smith noted. But he said the global trend was clearly away from mutually-owned financial institutions.
"The trend worldwide is that there is a pretty strong and significant move away from mutuality to proprietary companies and listings."

Sanlam, established in 1918, became the central vehicle for extending Afrikaner economic power in the apartheid era. Now it is rethinking its role and is divesting itself of many of its holdings, with the aim of becoming a focused financial services group.

It pioneered unbundling of South African conglomerates over three years ago with the break-up of Gencor Ltd, which spun off its non-mining interests. Today is it involved in the unbundling of consumer goods group Malbak Ltd.
Sanlam had accumulated capital of 9.3 billion rand at the end of 1996 and total assets of 132.9 billion.
